messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Simple workflow from landmarks to analysis?
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] Simple workflow from landmarks to analysis?
messages.body_plain:
If you are using the parser function in SlicerMorphR, the specimen labels are returned in the $ID object. They are also retained in the $LM array dimension names. You can use the standard R dimnames function to extract them as well.
After this point, you can add any categorical variable to your analysis. We don't support that in SlicerMorph, as there is no standard way of doing that.  Also, feel free to post these questions to our SlicerMorph user group, as this discussion is getting a bit off-topic for geomorph user group.

On Thursday, September 30, 2021 at 7:18:19 AM UTC-7 bcol...@umces.edu wrote:
> This was helpful, thanks. I have imported landmarks via parser and run GPA and PCA. Two follow-up questions -
>
> 1) Are the specimen names used when developing the GPA in slicermorph conserved when parsed into R from the data.log? If so, how do you recommend calling them when plotting a PCA?
> 2) Can categories be added after importing from slicermorph or should they be added after? Example, my individual landmarks are from 3 species and I want to conduct a by species analysis?
>
> On Saturday, September 25, 2021 at 4:50:18 PM UTC-4 mura...@gmail.com wrote:
> > I am away from my computer, but i think you want to check the supplemental material in our Slicermorph paper in MEE. It shows the necessary step for taking pseudo/semiLM from Slicermorph and use geomorph to align them via sliding (sections 3 through 7)
> > https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.13669
> >
> >
> >
> > On Saturday, September 25, 2021, Benjamin Colbert <bcol...@umces.edu> wrote:
> > > Murat - thanks! I went back to the slicerrmorph tutorials and used that to load GPA analyses into R as a 3d matrix. However, I think I understand from your message that I should run GPA in geomorph to allow my psuedolandmarks to slide. Is that true? If so, once I have those (using arrayspecs to turn my 7 fcsv files into a 3d matrix) I can GPA align them using gpagen. I could use some resources or sample code to go from here to then conducting an ANOVA or other statistical test to look at whether there are differences in shape by species. Thanks!
> > >
> > > On Friday, September 24, 2021 at 12:34:35 PM UTC-4 mura...@gmail.com wrote:
> > >>
> > >> There are a few ways you can do this. First off, if you are doing landmarking in SlicerMorph, I would discourage you using csv files to keep your coordinates. Instead use the fcsv, supported by Slicer which is csv plus some extra headers that is important for coordinate system definition, and other relevant things for your data. You can read this fcsv directly into Slicer, whereas you have to do import in csv.
> > >>
> > >> If you would like to read fcsv into R, it is a one-liner in straight R.
> > >>
> > >> lm = read.csv(file='path.to.fcsv', header=T, skip=2) and you have your lm coordinates along with their labels. You want to iterate over your samples.
> > >>
> > >> We did develop a very simple R package called SlicerMorphR to do these kinds of operations more streamlined. You can install via devtools::install_github("SlicerMorph/SlicerMorphR").
> > >> From that you can find functions like read.markups.fcsv, read.markups.json or write.markups.fcsv (if you want to convert data to Slicer). But more importantly if you already ran your GPA in SlicerMorph, you can simply point out to the analysis.log file in the output folder, and import all everything with a command
> > >> results=log_parses("path.to.analysis.log")
> > >> Please see the tutorial here: https://github.com/SlicerMorph/Tutorials/blob/main/GPA_3/README.md
> > >> There are a few benefits using the parser, particularly if you are working pseudo/semiLM, which in the current GM methodological paradigm are expected to be slid for better optimization. SlicerMorph will tag points generated via PseudoLMGenerator or SemiLMPatches with a different tag than anatomical LMs that are manually annotated. You will need the indices of these semi/pseudoLMs and 'fixed' LMs to pass the gpagen function of geomorph, if you are going to slide them. Relevant objects in the output of log_parser are $semi (boolean, are there any LMs tagged as semi/pseudoLMs?) and if it is true then there will be object called $semiLM that will contain the indices of LMs in the array that are tagged. The raw coordinates of data are saved in $LM. If this sounds complex, you can of course bypass all these and use your own method of tracking LMs and files.
> > >> We did not implement the sliding in SlicerMorph, because most people want to use R anyways for their inferential stats (python doesn't appear to be a popular for evolutionary morphologists for some reason).
> > >>
> > >> HTH,
> > >> M
> > >>
> > >> On Friday, September 24, 2021 at 7:30:01 AM UTC-7 bcol...@umces.edu wrote:
> > >>>
> > >>> I will look into arrayspecs, thanks.
> > >>> Not using any sliding, I am using fixed psuedolandmarks because my structure of interest has very few biologically relevant homologous locations for landmarks. Like I said, I'm still in learning . Thanks!
> > >>>
> > >>> On Friday, September 24, 2021 at 9:50:18 AM UTC-4 dca...@iastate.edu wrote:
> > >>>>
> > >>>> One can read a CSV file into R.  Depending on how the data are formatted in the CSV, one could use ‘arrayspecs’ in geomorph to put it in the proper format for downstream analyses.
> > >>>>
> > >>>>
> > >>>>
> > >>>> NOTE: If you have any semilandmarks in your data the GPA-alignment from SlicerMorph is not correct. Their approach does not perform any sliding. Thus it is advised to repeat the GPA in geomorph using the appropriate sliding of semilandmarks. Otherwise, one is explicitly determining that these are not curve or surface points, but actual, repeatable 3D fixed landmarks.

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] procD.pgls vs procD.lm for taxonomic variable
messages.subject_clean: [geomorph-r-package] procD.pgls vs procD.lm for taxonomic variable
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the response Dean.

By nested groups do you mean monophyletic? I assume you don’t mean nested within each other. The taxa I am comparing are indeed monophyletic, non-overlapping clades.

The BM question was related to my understanding that procD.pgls emulates a Brownian motion null model. I assume that patterns of trait distributions that fit expectations of BM would produce highly non-significant p values with procD.pgls but could produce significant p values with procD.lm. In contrast, trait distributions that are highly non-Brownian would, I assume, show significant p values under both procD.lm and procD.pgls.

I ask because while in my data the comparison shape~taxon is an example of the former, I have other traits that are an example of the latter.

Best Regards

Faysal Bibi

> On 29. Sep 2021, at 17:08, Adams, Dean [EEOB] <dca...@iastate.edu> wrote:
>

> Faysal,
>
> If your ‘groups’ in an anova-type linear model are nested taxonomic groups, then it makes little sense to compare them while accounting for the phylogeny. In fact, your highly non-significant result is precisely what I would expect if one tries to do so.
>
> The BM OU question is rather distinct from this. The anova compares groups, the BM/OU issue asks whether variation accumulates according to one or another evolutionary model.
>
> Dean
>
> Dr. Dean C. Adams
> Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology
> Director of Graduate Education, EEB Program
> Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology
> Iowa State University
> https://faculty.sites.iastate.edu/dcadams/
> phone: 515-294-3834
>
> From: geomorph-...@googlegroups.com<geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> On Behalf Of Faysal Bibi
> Sent: Wednesday, September 29, 2021 9:41 AM
> To: geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com>
> Subject: [geomorph-r-package] procD.pgls vs procD.lm for taxonomic variable
>
> Hello geomorphers
> A reviewer brought up a question that is quite simple but has me a bit puzzled. For a comparison of shape~taxon, is procD.pgls the appropriate test? Or does it make no sense to take phylogeny into account for a variable that is itself phylogenetic?
>
> This is for a dataset of 90 skulls representing 90 species from a single family, and the taxonomic variables are higher ranks like subfamilies or tribes. The question is whether significant differences in shape exist among these taxa (e.g. shape~tribe). If I use procD.lm, then I get p<0.001, presumably as a result of non-independence of the samples. Using procD.pgls, I get a p=0.9 or 1, which is perhaps not a surprise given I accounted for phylogeny, then proceeded to test for phylogenetic differences. I suppose this result (so close to p=1) also indicates that my data can be well explained by evolution under Brownian motion.
>
> Until now I have been using procD.pgls. Is the reviewer correct in asking me to consider using procD.lm instead to answer my question? Or could I perhaps present both results, saying that 'shape differences are present, but are entirely within expectations under Brownian motion' ?
>
> Also, if say a dataset were better described by an OU or Early Burst model of evolution, would a procD.pgls(shape~taxon) test then produce a significant p value?
>
> Thanks
> --

messages.subject: RRPP v 1.1.0 released on CRAN
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues,

I wish to alert you to some updates to the RRPP R package, the linear model workhorse for the geomorph package.  Version 1.1.0 is now available on CRAN and Github (mlcollyer/RRPP), and for the moment, both versions are the same.  This is a minor release.  Although most releases are patch releases — fix bugs or modify functions — this minor release largely updates all support code to be compliant with R 4.1 updates, and is, therefore, more comprehensive, even if no changes are apparent.  I urge you to update this package, even if geomorph appears to be working fine.  One of the issues we encountered is dropped data names, especially for data that could be coerced into either a vector or matrix, which renders indexing either impossible, or worse, erroneous (in which case a result could be produced that shouldn’t be produced).  Updates should not affect geomorph functions, but it is possible that our battery of tests missed an issue.  If you find an issue, please alert me.  With large-scale coding changes, additional patch updates might be needed.

In spite of the R 4.1 update spurring the RRPP 1.1.0 release, we also have a new function (tool) for a leave-one-out cross-validation procedure (looCV), which can be used on lm.rrpp, procD.lm, or procD.pgls linear model fits.  This function is based on the procedure described by Cardini and Polly (2020) <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11692-020-09494-x> and should be similar to the tools just published by Thioulouse and colleagues <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11692-021-09550-0> in the ade4 package, which work in conjunction with other analytical tools there.  These papers address more specifically the spurious between-group graphical differences that might manifest from between-groups PCA (bgPCA) of high-dimensional data, even in spite of no true group differences, as pointed out by Cardini et al. (2019) <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11692-019-09487-5>.  Our function is a little different in that it can be used with any linear model (including one that use GLS estimation) where PCA is performed on the fitted values from the model.  This function is most effective when used with its S3 plotting associated function, plot.looCV, which plots side-by-side the PC plot of a fitted model — the same as plot(fit, type = “PC”, …) — and the plot of cross-validated scores.  (If they are similar, it supports the real differences between groups; if they are different, it supports the conclusion that apparent group differences are spurious in the low-dimensional projection.)

The RRPP::looCV function has a couple of differences compared to the tools in the ade4 package, which are explained in the associated help file.  This function should work well in the RRPP/geomorph environment, without having to reformat results from lm.rrpp/procD.lm/procD.pgls objects (which also means it can be used with PGLS analyses).

With warm regards!

Mike (on behalf of Mike and Dean)

messages.subject: Error in plot.gm.prcomp
messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I am trying to plot the first and second PC axes from a PCA I just ran on the symmetric component of my shape data. When I try to use the function plot.gm.prcomp though, R gives me an error saying it could not find the function even though I have activated geomorph in this R session. I have also double-checked that all my packages are updated and that R and RStudio are updated (so this is geomorph v4.0.1), tried uninstalling and reinstalling geomorph, restarting R, restarting my whole computer, and still no luck.

I am extra confused because I can successfully use the gmShiny app on my local computer and produce PCA plots (which if I understand correctly should rely on plot.gm.prcomp on the back-end), but I cannot use gmShiny for this particular plot since my data has more than ten groups.

Have I missed something, or does this indicate something is wrong with the package?

Any advice would be greatly appreciated!

Mariah

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Error in plot.gm.prcomp
messages.body_plain:
The function has not been deleted.  It is an S3 generic function.  One uses

plot(my.PCA)

and not

plot.gm.prcomp(my.PCA)

The “.gm.prcomp” part of the function instructs R when somebody uses plot(), for gm.prcomp class objects.

You can learn more here <http://adv-r.had.co.nz/S3.html>.

Also look at the gm.prcomp file, and notice that the examples do not use plot.gm.prcomp, but use plot only.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject: Question about pairwise analysis for univariate data
messages.subject_clean: Question about pairwise analysis for univariate data
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

My question relates purely to the RRPP package rather than geomorph, I hope that isn't a problem!

I have been using the RRPP package to run a phylogenetic ANOVA on my data, using the model:

Fullmod <- lm.rrpp(R1 ~ E1 + E2 + E3 + E4, data = Data, print.progress = T, Cov = Finalvcv,  RRPP = T, SS.type = "II", iter = 999999)

Where R1 is our univariate response variable (an average value recorded for each species) and E1-E4 are explanatory environmental variables.

When I run the model, E1 has a significant effect (r^2 = 0.44, F = 12.1, p < 0.0001). From plotting the data, it seems likely that one particular category in E1 is very distinct, and likely driving this pattern.

However, when I run a pairwise analysis to look for differences in means between groups, using:

PW <- pairwise(Fullmod, groups = Data$E1)
summary(PW, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "dist")

No pairwise difference is significant, and we get very high p-values, even between groups with very different R1 values.

Is the pairwise test I am using appropriate? Or is there some other reason why the pairwise test is not detecting differences between groups?

I notice in this thread <https://groups.google.com/g/geomorph-r-package/c/VbHHzktnOPE>, it is mentioned that there could be a conceptual issue with using RRPP pairwise test to analyse univariate data. Could this be causing the issue?

Thanks for all your help,

Edd Page

messages.body_plain:
Dear Edd,

I think with your example, I would need to maybe see the data to see if there is an issue, rather than speculate causes.  If you do not mind sharing (if it is small enough to send), you could send it to me directly outside of the googlegroup and I can take a look.

Here are some other things to try to see if you get different answers, to help elucidate if this might be a bug:

1. Try different types of SS and see if the result changes much.
2. Try without the covariance matrix and see if the result makes more sense.
3. Append a column of 0s to R1, e.g., R2 <- cbind(R1, 0), and replace this matrix for R1 in the analysis.

Option 3 might not surprise me as we just had issues with single variables and R losing names when coercing vectors into matrices or vice versa.  By forcing a matrix, you should get the same ANOVA results but if the pairwise results suddenly make sense, then it might be an indexing problem caused by lost names affecting your pairwise results.

Regardless, I am happy to take a look if you are willing to share data.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.subject: Repeated Morphology for Individuals over Time
messages.subject_clean: Repeated Morphology for Individuals over Time
messages.body_plain:
Hi all!

I am working with a data set of repeat measures of morphometrics on 64 cutthroat trout. I have 4 different replicate measurements of the same 24 landmarks on these 64 fish. I am trying to closely examine how each individual changes in their shape over time relative to the mean, but I am struggling with using multiple levels of classifiers in my analysis and using the advanced.procD.lm function.

Does anyone have any advice for approaching the formatting of data for this problem? I am really sorry if this is a dumb/obvious question. I have primarily taught myself these methods and coding throughout my M.Sc.

Any advice is greatly appreciated!!

Thank you!
Taylor

https://github.com/geomorphR/geomorph
https://github.com/mlcollyer/RRPP

The vignette here has been supplied to assist users in running the analyses that were possible through advanced.procD.lm: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/geomorph/vignettes/geomorph.assistance.html.

Not a dumb question, and this list is to help people. I've found the help files and vignettes super useful but I'd also encourage you to reach out once you review them if you run into more problems.

Best,
Bryan
